hints: Look at what is attacking the carbon in iodoethane, water provides a nucleophile, not an electrophile.
Hydrolysis of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{I}$ releases iodide ions, $\text{I}^-$, into solution for silver ions to trap.
Recall the silver halide colours from the test: chloride is white, bromide is cream, so what is left for iodide?
walkthrough:
**Identify the organic change**

Think of water as a nucleophile attacking the slightly positive carbon. The C-I bond breaks and $\text{OH}^-$ replaces $\text{I}^-$. That is nucleophilic substitution.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{I} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{H}^+ + \text{I}^-$$

**See why a precipitate forms**

The released $\text{I}^-$ meets $\text{Ag}^+$ from aqueous silver nitrate. They combine to make insoluble silver iodide.

$$\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{I}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgI}(s)$$

**Recall the precipitate colour**

Learn this colour trio by heart for the silver nitrate test. $\text{AgCl}$ is white, $\text{AgBr}$ is cream, and $\text{AgI}$ is yellow.

So we have nucleophilic substitution plus a yellow precipitate.

options.A: Incorrect on both parts. It is not electrophilic substitution because a nucleophile ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) attacks the electron-deficient carbon, and cream is the colour for $\text{AgBr}$, not $\text{AgI}$.
options.B: Half right on colour but wrong on mechanism. Yellow is correct for $\text{AgI}$, but haloalkane hydrolysis is nucleophilic substitution, not electrophilic substitution which is typical of benzene.
options.C: Half right on mechanism but wrong on colour. Nucleophilic substitution is correct, but cream precipitate indicates bromide ($\text{AgBr}$). Iodoethane gives iodide, so $\text{AgI}$ is yellow.
options.D: Correct on both parts. Water acts as a nucleophile replacing iodine in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{I}$, so nucleophilic substitution, and the $\text{I}^-$ formed gives yellow $\text{AgI}$ precipitate with $\text{AgNO}_3$.
